{"id": "68:43/q11", "question": "Why are they called to prostrate on that Day?", "turns_on": "Whether the scene is framed chiefly as test, rebuke, or permission for true worshippers.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q11/p1", "position": "The call tests and distinguishes sincere believers from hypocrites.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it honors the former and exposes the latter; Qatāda says believers' act humiliates hypocrites; al-Ḥasan says Muslims remain for testing."}, {"id": "68:43/q11/p2", "position": "The call rebukes their earlier refusal and increases regret; it is no new legal duty.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Elmalılı and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ emphasize rebuke; Elmalılı rejects Abū Muslim's claim Resurrection is impossible for a summons because rebuke requires no legal command. Islahi says the summons exposes their lack of excuse."}, {"id": "68:43/q11/p3", "position": "The summons gives sincere worshippers permission to prostrate.", "reasons": "The Prophetic report via Qatāda and Qatāda's own account say believers are allowed to prostrate; the rest cannot."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q12", "question": "When was the earlier summons to prostrate?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning's immediate scene is Resurrection, life's end, or worldly incapacity.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q12/p1", "position": "It was during worldly life, when response was possible.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explicitly says both the summons and safety refer to worldly life; Ibn ʿAbbās contrasts former security with present fear. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the clause parenthetic recollection. Al-Qushayrī says recalling the old call makes proof decisive and regret sharper."}, {"id": "68:43/q12/p2", "position": "The warning may also meet them at the end of life or beginning of the next.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī leaves both boundaries possible. Abū Muslim proposes the last day of a life, when angels bring no good news and late conversion fails, with 25:22 and 6:158; another explanation has a dying patient unable to rise."}, {"id": "68:43/q12/p3", "position": "It can describe illness, old age or incapacity while still in this life.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim proposes bodily incapacity following prior soundness; Elmalılı permits this worldly reading but rejects exclusion of Resurrection."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q13", "question": "What does the earlier call to prostrate ask of them?", "turns_on": "Whether sujūd denotes bodily prostration, prayer, all obedience, or inward surrender.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q13/p1", "position": "It asks for the prescribed ritual prayers, represented by their prostration.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī and Qatāda identify obligatory prayer; some specify all five. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr identifies the summons to congregational prayer. Bursawī says prayer contains prostrations. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī dismisses this reading."}, {"id": "68:43/q13/p2", "position": "It asks for literal prostration to God and worship of Him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says no impediment then; the call was freely rejected despite ability. Some accounts make worldly sincere prostration the condition for prostration on Judgment Day."}, {"id": "68:43/q13/p3", "position": "Prostration stands for all acts of obedience or the summons of religious obligation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports some interpreters: prostration is greatest obedience and the later test. Al-Qurṭubī says the explanations are close; al-Ālūsī gives the wider obligation reading; Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbdallāh speak of obeying commands and avoiding prohibitions."}, {"id": "68:43/q13/p4", "position": "It means inward surrender and readiness to receive the world of light.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says their faculties and readiness were still present, allowing future happiness."}, {"id": "68:43/q13/p5", "position": "It summons people to worship God alone in submission to His lordship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the parenthesis recalls this; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links afterlife felicity to worldly acknowledgment of God's sole lordship."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q14", "question": "How was the earlier summons delivered?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording points to the public prayer call, wider divine and prophetic commands, or the afterlife caller.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q14/p1", "position": "Through the adhān and iqāma, especially 'Come to success' or 'Come to prayer'.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm al-Taymī names adhān and iqāma; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says they heard 'Come to success' yet did not come; Ibn ʿAbbās gives hearing and ignoring the call; Bursawī also cites scholars' invitations."}, {"id": "68:43/q14/p2", "position": "Through God's command, the Prophet, prophets, religious teachers, or the imposed religious duty.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports divine commands to establish prayer and Prophetic invitation; the Prophet's instruction to pray five times, fast, give zakāt and obey promised Paradise. He cites the report that a servant is nearest God in prostration; al-Nasafī says prophets called; al-Biqāʿī says callers to God."}, {"id": "68:43/q14/p3", "position": "By a caller who invites prostration on Resurrection Day.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Qatāda describe that caller; the summons publicly exposes hypocrites."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q15", "question": "What does سَٰلِمُونَ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether safety refers to bodily health, freedom from fear, or inward capacity.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q15/p1", "position": "They were healthy, physically sound and able, without impediment to prostration.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says no obstacle; Ibn ʿAṭiyya contrasts their then flexible backs with later fused vertebrae; al-Biqāʿī says arrogance rather than weakness stopped them; Ibn ʿĀshūr defines salāma as absence of defects and disease. Elmalılı stresses safety and freedom."}, {"id": "68:43/q15/p2", "position": "They were free from fear, unlike the fearful summons now.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly contrasts worldly security with present fear; al-Ṭabarī's link to 11:20 describes their inability to heed in both lives."}, {"id": "68:43/q15/p3", "position": "Their faculties and readiness for inward felicity were intact.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says they were able to receive the influx of the world of light and gain happiness."}, {"id": "68:43/q15/p4", "position": "They were free of the afflictions that later destroyed the soul's capacity to answer truth.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī offers this before the simpler physical-ability interpretation."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q16", "question": "What is the grammar of وَهُمْ سَٰلِمُونَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q16/p1", "position": "It is a waw-marked circumstantial clause describing those summoned in worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives its subject as the subject of the second yudʿawn; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the waw marks the circumstance."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q17", "question": "What warning about congregational prayer is drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning targets attendance at congregation specifically or neglect of prescribed prayer generally.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q17/p1", "position": "The verse warns those who hear the congregational prayer call but fail to attend.", "reasons": "Kaʿb swears that it was revealed specifically about absentees; al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī and Ibn al-Jawzī apply the warning. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym came despite paralysis, urging even crawling; Ibn al-Musayyib answered despite a threat from Ṭāriq. Al-Qurṭubī points to his earlier discussion of congregational prayer's obligation."}, {"id": "68:43/q17/p2", "position": "The verse concerns the five obligatory prayers when their call is made.", "reasons": "Kaʿb's version in al-Durr names five prayers; other authorities identify prescribed prayer and its call."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q18", "question": "Why repeat the summons to prostrate explicitly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q18/p1", "position": "The explicit wording in place of a pronoun emphasizes the earlier summons.", "reasons": "Bursawī also allows that the wording marks prostration as standing for prayer and its prostrations; al-Ālūsī agrees on emphasis."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q19", "question": "Why single out prostration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q19/p1", "position": "It is the greatest act of obedience and serves as the decisive afterlife test.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the figurative reading to some interpreters; Bursawī states the ranking directly. A Prophetic report cited by Bursawī says the servant is closest to the Lord while prostrating."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q20", "question": "What unspoken response follows the earlier summons?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q20/p1", "position": "Their refusal to answer is omitted because the context makes it evident.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī states the ellipsis; many explanations explicitly say they refused though capable."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q21", "question": "How do the two verses pair ability and inability?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q21/p1", "position": "The passage uses iḥtibāk: present inability implies omitted former ability, and former safety implies omitted present unsafety.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī states both halves of the correspondence."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q22", "question": "What moral reversal does their condition teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q22/p1", "position": "Their former arrogance and refusal return as helplessness, shame and regret.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls it punishment opposite to worldly crimes; Elmalılı says they thought sinners wiser than believers and now desire what they refused; Islahi says their own bodies testify to lack of excuse; Study Quran says some Arabs deemed prostration humiliating but meet greater humiliation. {"id": "68:43/q23", "question": "What links this scene to other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different scriptural parallels for the scene.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q23/p1", "position": "11:20 parallels their failure to hear or see in life and to prostrate now.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly draw the link."}, {"id": "68:43/q23/p2", "position": "70:43–44 parallels emergence from graves with downcast eyes and ignominy.", "reasons": "Islahi says the parallel clarifies the exposed-shin Day as severe upheaval; Muqātil connects lowered eyes on seeing the Fire to al-Qalam."}, {"id": "68:43/q23/p3", "position": "89:23–25 parallels the sinner's useless late wish to have prepared for true life.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects that wish to the missed time for prostration."}, {"id": "68:43/q23/p4", "position": "83:6 is invoked for the long standing before God.", "reasons": "The report to ʿUmar names forty years of standing."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q24", "question": "How does this passage fit its surrounding argument?", "turns_on": "The sources emphasize different surrounding themes.", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q24/p1", "position": "It interrupts the argument about alleged partners to show that only worldly submission to God's sole lordship yields afterlife happiness.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the alleged partners cannot provide felicity or intercession at Resurrection."}, {"id": "68:43/q24/p2", "position": "It depicts a cataclysmic Day that overturns dreams of worldly luxury.", "reasons": "Islahi places the refusal to prostrate within that reversal and reads 70:43–44 as its parallel."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q25", "question": "What accounts for the Qur'an's inimitable expression?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q25/p1", "position": "Its eloquent wording, exact placement, sound meanings and ordered joining of diverse excellences exceed human capacity.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī says substitution damages meaning or style; al-Burhān and al-Itqān enumerate doctrine, worship, law, ethics, exhortation, past and future reports, and proof joined to conclusion. They say only divine knowledge unites these qualities."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q26", "question": "How did opponents characterize the Qur'an despite its effect on them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q26/p1", "position": "They called it poetry, sorcery or dictated ancient legends while acknowledging its sweetness.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī and later compilations say poetry was inferred from order and sorcery from inability to match it; the dictated-lore charge conflicted with knowledge that Muhammad was unlettered and had no nearby dictation helper, compared with 25:5."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q27", "question": "What does the report about al-Walīd's deliberation say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q27/p1", "position": "After reflection, al-Walīd called the Qur'an human speech or sorcery.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī tentatively identifies him; the Qur'an recounts his thought and claims in 74:18, 74:24–25. Al-Burhān says frustration and stubbornness drove the claim."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q28", "question": "Why do near-synonyms matter in Qur'anic wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q28/p1", "position": "Words that overlap retain distinct meanings, so their exact placement matters.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī lists knowledge/recognition, praise/gratitude, and stinginess/miserliness; he says maʿrifa takes one object, ʿilm two, and one says 'recognize God' but 'know God' with an attribute such as just or powerful."}]}
{"id": "68:43/q29", "question": "How did the practice of combining readings in one completion develop?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:43/q29/p1", "position": "Early readers completed one transmission at a time; combining readings in one completion became established later.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says earlier authorities largely omitted the topic; al-Ṣafrawī only hinted at it. He attributes omission to intensive repeated study: al-Ḥuṣrī reportedly made ninety completions over ten years, al-Kattānī was kept with ʿĀṣim by Ibn Mujāhid, and al-Wāsiṭī spent years on multiple completions. Some imams disliked combination as novel, but it became accepted."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q01", "question": "Who were Thamūd?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q01/p1", "position": "They were the people of the prophet Ṣāliḥ.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Biqāʿī identify their prophet as Ṣāliḥ. Bursevī says they were Arabs living at al-Ḥijr between Syria and the Ḥijāz, on the Syrian pilgrims' route."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q02", "question": "How is the verb 'they were destroyed' read?", "turns_on": "Which verbal form or, in the separate report, which consonantal reading is transmitted.", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q02/p1", "position": "The common reading is passive, fa-uhlikū, 'they were destroyed.'", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this the majority reading; al-Samīn calls it the general reading."}, {"id": "69:5/q02/p2", "position": "Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads active fa-halakū, 'they perished.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn derives it from the triliteral halaka; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also report the reading."}, {"id": "69:5/q02/p3", "position": "A separate later passage has lā yakhfā with yāʾ or lā takhfā with tāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī reports Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī for yāʾ, other readers for tāʾ, and judges both sound; this variant concerns a later verse, not the wording of 69:5."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q03", "question": "Why is destruction expressed in the passive?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q03/p1", "position": "The passive foregrounds the terrifying destruction, while God as its agent is already understood.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the tangible horror receives attention; Bursevī says God is the known actor, so the event matters; al-Ālūsī explicitly says God destroyed Thamūd."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q04", "question": "What does the root and descriptive force of al-ṭāghiya convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q04/p1", "position": "It conveys exceeding a proper limit, including excessive force, severity, or rebellion.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj illustrates excess by the overflowing water of 69:11 and compares ʿĀd's fierce wind in 69:6. Al-Wāḥidī says anything ṭāghī exceeds its measure. Al-Rāzī adduces 69:11 and 53:17 for exceeding bounds. Al-Qurṭubī and Iṣlāḥī cite the floodwater in 69:11; Iṣlāḥī also cites Thamūd's rebellion in 91:11. Al-Nasafī and Study Quran stress extreme severity, and Elmalılı allows either a transgressing event or tyranny."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q05", "question": "What is al-ṭāghiya by which Thamūd were destroyed?", "turns_on": "Whether bi-l-ṭāghiya gives the physical instrument or event of destruction, the people's moral cause, an agent whose act implicated them, or its location; the parallel with ʿĀd's wind and the bāʾ's force are central arguments.", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q05/p1", "position": "An overwhelming cry or blast destroyed them.", "reasons": "Qatāda repeatedly calls it a cry beyond ordinary cries, sometimes one cry that silenced and killed them; al-Qurṭubī connects the single cry of 54:31. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya favor it because 69:6 similarly names ʿĀd's destructive wind. Al-Biqāʿī and Bursevī say earth and hearts trembled. Ibn Kathīr joins the cry and quake, and Elmalılı calls the same event a cry, thunderous blast and accompanying quake. Al-Ālūsī relates the shriek to 11:67 and the thunderbolt to 41:17; al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī reconcile quake accounts as accompanying or caused by the shriek. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors a mode of destruction in the following sequence; Study Quran cites 11:67 and 54:31. Al-Durr also reports Ibn ʿAbbās for the cry, despite other transmissions of his view."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p2", "position": "Their own transgression, disbelief, or sins brought their destruction.", "reasons": "Muqātil links rebellion to rejecting Ṣāliḥ. Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba give transgression or unbelief; Mujāhid says sins, while Ibn Zayd specifies rebellion against God's signs and Book and cites 91:11. Al-Wāḥidī attributes this view to most exegetes and grammarians, including al-Kalbī, Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid. Al-Ḥasan and others take the form as a verbal noun; al-Baghawī also allows an adjective for their outrageous act. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites Sūrat al-Shams; Study Quran says this moral cause can coexist with a destructive calamity. Reports differ on Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd and al-Kalbī, who also appear with other explanations."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p3", "position": "An overwhelming earthquake or upheaval destroyed them.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq prefer a quake. Al-Bayḍāwī cites their denial of the Calamity in 69:4; Kuranyolu links their denial and disobedience to 7:73–79 and 11:61–68. Asad points to 7:78 and translates the event as upheaval. Al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī associate or causally connect the quake with the blast, the latter citing 7:78; Elmalılı and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ list it among Qur'anic descriptions."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p4", "position": "A thunderbolt, perhaps a lightning strike, destroyed them.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās name a thunderbolt. Al-Ālūsī cites 41:17 alongside the shriek; Elmalılı includes a thunderous blast among descriptions; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran list Qur'anic thunderbolt accounts, the latter citing 41:13 and 51:44. Iṣlāḥī infers from al-Dhāriyāt a thunderbolt from striped winter clouds and says God can turn ordinary lightning into a weapon."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p5", "position": "It names the calamity or severe destructive event without specifying its form.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī first calls it an overwhelming calamity. Al-Naḥḥās reports an overwhelming event or group. Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Bayḍāwī and Study Quran speak of an event exceeding ordinary severity; al-Rāzī cites 69:11 and 53:17. Al-Qurṭubī supplies a

Study Quran says an individual may have persuaded the people to hamstring the camel, citing 91:13 and 54:23–30."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p8", "position": "It names a transgressive faction among Thamūd.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says a faction plotted the camel's hamstringing and brought destruction through its ill omen. Study Quran allows a powerful minority that persuaded the people to kill the camel."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p9", "position": "It names a woman who hamstrung the she-camel.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī transmits this specifically from Ibn Zayd, whereas other reports identify an unnamed or male individual."}, {"id": "69:5/q05/p10", "position": "It names the place where Thamūd were destroyed.", "reasons": "Al-Karmānī reports this view through al-Itqān."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q06", "question": "How does the form al-ṭāghiya work grammatically in these explanations?", "turns_on": "Whether the feminine form is a verbal noun, modifies a suppressed noun, or intensifies a designation for a person.", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q06/p1", "position": "It can be a feminine verbal noun meaning transgression.", "reasons": "Language authorities, Abū Isḥāq and al-Zajjāj compare ʿāfiya and ʿāqiba. Al-Ḥasan gives the same analysis; al-Samīn adduces ṭughwā in 91:11. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī say this parsing fits the ensuing ʿĀd clause poorly."}, {"id": "69:5/q06/p2", "position": "It can be an adjective with an omitted noun, such as cry, event, or deed.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports Qatāda's omitted 'cry'; al-Rāzī supplies an omitted event; al-Qurṭubī supplies deed or event; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī allow a quality of the rebellious act."}, {"id": "69:5/q06/p3", "position": "For a person or faction, the feminine form can be an intensive designation.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī apply this to the camel's killer; al-Qurṭubī compares other personal designations, such as narrator, prodigy, scholar and genealogist."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q07", "question": "What does the bāʾ in bi-l-ṭāghiya express?", "turns_on": "Whether the named thing is an instrument of destruction or a reason for it; al-Qāḍī disputes the proposed causal wording.", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q07/p1", "position": "With the cry it marks the instrument by which they were destroyed.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn compares 'I worked with the adze'; al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya infer instrument from ʿĀd's wind in 69:6."}, {"id": "69:5/q07/p2", "position": "With transgression, deed, or person it marks the cause of their destruction.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this for all non-cry interpretations. Al-Qāḍī objects that a causal sense should have used wording meaning 'for it' rather than bi-ṭāghiya."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q08", "question": "How does this clause relate to the account of ʿĀd in the next verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired clauses need to name the same kind of cause, as the following wind appears to name the means of punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q08/p1", "position": "Both clauses name the punishment or physical means of destruction.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī use ʿĀd's wind in 69:6 to favor a Thamūd calamity. Al-Zajjāj and the reported Zamakhsharī argue the clauses otherwise lose balance; al-Ālūsī specifies that the balance concerns parallel causes, since both peoples could be called transgressors. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī also find the verbal-noun reading discordant. Al-Jishumī identifies blast and wind and notes the account begins and ends with 'day'. Al-Biqāʿī says a shared denial is followed by distinct punishments."}, {"id": "69:5/q08/p2", "position": "The first clause can give Thamūd's rebellion while the second gives ʿĀd's wind.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī transmit or allow the verbal-noun analysis while noting its poor fit with the next clause. Study Quran explicitly lets moral cause and destructive calamity both apply."}]}
{"id": "69:5/q09", "question": "How are the cry, earthquake, and thunderbolt accounts related?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:5/q09/p1", "position": "They can describe one event: a shriek accompanied by or causing an earthquake, also described as a thunderous blast.", "reasons": "Bursevī says cry and quake are the same event. Al-Ālūsī says the shriek caused the quake, so verses can cite a near or remote cause; he cites 11:67, 7:78 and 41:17. {"id": "69:6/q08", "question": "What does ṣarṣar mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣarṣar is traced to cold, to the wind's sound, to force, or to scorching heat; some sources explicitly allow two senses together or as alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "69:6/q08/p1", "position": "Bitterly or severely cold wind.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others give cold; Qatāda says it pierced hearts. {"id": "69:6/q09", "question": "What does the doubled form ṣarṣar add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:6/q09/p1", "position": "Doubling can convey repeated action or intensity.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj raises repetition for ṣarṣar and compares qalqala, repeated lifting, with aqalla, lifting, and doubled sound forms ṣarṣar and ṣalṣal with ṣar and ṣal. {"id": "69:6/q11", "question": "What does ʿātiya say about the wind?", "turns_on": "The target of the wind's 'rebellion' may be its ordinary bounds or angelic keepers, or the people it overwhelmed; some explain the keeper language figuratively.", "positions": [{"id": "69:6/q11/p1", "position": "It was exceptionally violent, exceeding ordinary force, measure, or bounds.", "reasons": "Muqātil says it exceeded its stores without pity. {"id": "69:6/q12", "question": "How does calling the wind 'rebellious' work as a figure of speech?", "turns_on": "Whether the figurative mechanism is direct metaphor, emphatic simile, or a representative image that can function metonymically.", "positions": [{"id": "69:6/q12/p1", "position": "Rebellion is a metaphor for the wind's extreme force and excess.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says the report's language may express exceptional intensity; his gloss uses rebellion metaphorically. {"id": "69:6/q13", "question": "How do the clauses about Thamūd and ʿĀd relate?", "turns_on": "The sources identify different features of the pairing: cause, matched words for excess, and the surrounding day frame.", "positions": [{"id": "69:6/q13/p1", "position": "They name parallel causes of destruction: Thamūd's overpowering cry and ʿĀd's wind.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers the cry as the calamity named for Thamūd, matching ʿĀd's wind here. {"id": "69:9/q02", "question": "How is وَمَن قَبْلَهُ read, and whom does it include?", "turns_on": "The qāf and bāʾ vowels distinguish temporal precedence from spatial company, though some notes also allow ‘with him’ under the fatḥa wording; the context determines whether a general expression includes believers.", "positions": [{"id": "69:9/q02/p1", "position": "With fatḥa on qāf and still bāʾ, it means earlier unbelieving peoples.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī lists most Medinan, Kufan and Meccan readers except Kisāʾī; other sources list Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim in some transmissions, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and others. Ubayy’s and Ibn Masʿūd’s ‘those with him,’ Abū Mūsā’s ‘alongside him,’ Ṭalḥa’s ‘around him,’ and a reported ‘those following him’ support the spatial sense. Ḥasan combines those before and those with him; Ibn Jurayj interprets the fatḥa wording as company. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim prefer the companion reading; Ṭabarī validates both."}]}
